content: Viral epidemics and pandemics, such as the 2009 H1N1 influenza pandemic, the 2003 SARS outbreak, and the 2019 COVID-19 pandemic caused by SARS-CoV-2, represent significant global health threats. While antiviral medications and vaccines are critical tools, they may not be sufficient to fully prevent the spread of these respiratory viruses. This review, an update of a Cochrane Review last published in 2020, evaluates the effectiveness of physical interventions in reducing or interrupting the transmission of acute respiratory viruses, incorporating data from studies conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic. To conduct this review, databases such as CENTRAL, PubMed, Embase, and CINAHL were searched in October 2022, along with trial registries. Randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and cluster-RCTs examining physical interventions—including screening at entry points, isolation, quarantine, physical distancing, personal protective equipment, hand hygiene, face masks, eye protection, and gargling—were included. Standard Cochrane methodologies were employed for data collection and analysis. This update includes 11 new RCTs and cluster-RCTs, involving 610,872 participants, bringing the total number of included trials to 78. Six of the new trials were conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic in countries such as Mexico, Denmark, Bangladesh, England, and Norway. Many studies were conducted during periods of lower respiratory virus circulation, such as non-epidemic influenza seasons or the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, which may differ from the high transmission context of COVID-19. The studies were conducted in diverse settings, including suburban schools, hospital wards in high-income countries, crowded urban areas in low-income countries, and immigrant neighborhoods in high-income countries. Adherence to interventions was often low, and the risk of bias in the included trials was generally high or unclear. Medical/Surgical Masks vs. No Masks Twelve trials (10 of which were cluster-RCTs) compared the use of medical or surgical masks to no masks in preventing respiratory viral illnesses. Two trials involved healthcare workers, while 10 were conducted in community settings. The evidence suggests that wearing masks in the community likely makes little to no difference in reducing influenza-like illness (ILI) or COVID-19-like illness compared to not wearing masks (risk ratio [RR] 0.95, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.84 to 1.09; moderate-certainty evidence). Similarly, wearing masks probably has little to no effect on laboratory-confirmed influenza or SARS-CoV-2 infections (RR 1.01, 95% CI 0.72 to 1.42; moderate-certainty evidence). Harms associated with mask use were rarely measured or reported, and the certainty of evidence for harms was very low. N95/P2 Respirators vs. Medical/Surgical Masks Five trials compared N95/P2 respirators with medical or surgical masks, with four conducted in healthcare settings and one in a household setting. The evidence is very uncertain regarding the effects of N95/P2 respirators compared to medical/surgical masks on clinical respiratory illness (RR 0.70, 95% CI 0.45 to 1.10; very low-certainty evidence). For ILI, N95/P2 respirators may be slightly more effective than medical/surgical masks (RR 0.82, 95% CI 0.66 to 1.03; low-certainty evidence). However, for laboratory-confirmed influenza, N95/P2 respirators likely make little to no difference compared to medical/surgical masks (RR 1.10, 95% CI 0.90 to 1.34; moderate-certainty evidence). Restricting the analysis to healthcare workers did not alter these findings. Discomfort associated with wearing masks or respirators was noted in several studies, but harms were poorly measured and reported. A recently published RCT involving 1009 healthcare workers across four countries found that medical/surgical masks were non-inferior to N95 respirators in preventing respiratory viral infections among those providing direct care to COVID-19 patients. Hand Hygiene vs. Control Nineteen trials compared hand hygiene interventions to control groups without interventions. These studies were conducted in settings such as schools, childcare centers, and homes. Hand hygiene interventions were associated with a 14% relative reduction in acute respiratory infections (ARIs) compared to controls (RR 0.86, 95% CI 0.81 to 0.90; moderate-certainty evidence). This translates to a reduction from 380 cases per 1000 people to 327 cases per 1000 people. However, when more strictly defined outcomes such as ILI and laboratory-confirmed influenza were analyzed, the intervention showed little to no effect (RR 0.94 for ILI and RR 0.91 for laboratory-confirmed influenza; low-certainty evidence). Pooled data from 19 trials suggested that hand hygiene may reduce respiratory illness by 11% (RR 0.89, 95% CI 0.83 to 0.94; low-certainty evidence), but there was significant heterogeneity across studies. Harms associated with hand hygiene were rarely measured or reported. Other Interventions No RCTs were identified that evaluated the effectiveness of gowns, gloves, face shields, or screening at entry points in preventing respiratory viral transmission. Authors' Conclusions The high risk of bias, variability in outcome measurements, and low adherence to interventions in many studies limit the ability to draw firm conclusions. While additional RCTs were conducted during the COVID-19 pandemic, there remains a relative lack of high-quality evidence on the effectiveness of physical interventions, particularly masking, and the impact of adherence on their effectiveness. The evidence suggests uncertainty regarding the effects of face masks, with low to moderate certainty, indicating that the true effect may differ from the observed estimates. Pooled results from RCTs did not demonstrate a clear reduction in respiratory viral infections with the use of medical/surgical masks. Similarly, no significant differences were observed between medical/surgical masks and N95/P2 respirators in healthcare settings for routine care. Hand hygiene likely provides a modest reduction in respiratory illness, but its effect on more specific outcomes such as ILI and laboratory-confirmed influenza is less clear. Harms associated with physical interventions were under-investigated. There is a need for large, well-designed RCTs to evaluate the effectiveness of these interventions across various settings and populations, with a focus on adherence and its impact on outcomes, particularly in vulnerable groups such as the elderly and young children.
